keyTakeaways: Which reply is correct is fixed by the verb they used: te extraño / te echo de menos take yo también; me haces falta cannot take it at all, because the RAE's DPD records faltar as intransitive in every sense.
Spanish does postpose the particle — in a 120-sentence Tatoeba census, también was clause-final 30.0% of the time, medial 33.3% and sentence-initial 36.7%.
The real asymmetry with English is optionality, not placement: Spanish may omit the subject pronoun, so writing yo is itself the focus signal English has no way to send.

Register drives it — yo is rank 229 in Leipzig's 3M-sentence Spanish news corpus but rank 1,761 in Spanish Wikipedia, and a 2025 study found overt subject rates of 2.9%–22% predicted by how speech-like the text is.
214 miss-you pages on /missyou-gf carry a median 88-word letter, so a page suits a paragraph; a four-word chat reply needs none of it.

faqs.question: How do you say 'I miss you too' in Spanish?
faqs.answer: If they wrote te extraño, reply yo también te extraño. If they wrote te echo de menos, reply yo también te echo de menos. If they wrote me haces falta, reply tú también me haces falta — yo también does not work with that verb, because the RAE's Diccionario panhispánico de dudas records faltar and hacer falta as intransitive in every sense.

faqs.question: Is 'yo también te extraño' or 'te extraño también' more correct?
faqs.answer: Both are correct Spanish. In a 120-sentence Tatoeba census sampled on 2026-09-28, también was clause-final in 30.0% of sentences, so postposing it is ordinary. The difference is that te extraño también leaves the subject slot empty and can be read as 'I miss you as well as other things', while yo también te extraño puts the addition squarely on you.

faqs.question: Why do Spanish speakers write 'yo' when the verb already says 'I'?
faqs.answer: Because it is optional, and optional material is read as contrastive. In the Leipzig Corpora Collection's 3-million-sentence Spanish news corpus, yo ranks 229th with 22,562 hits; in the Spanish Wikipedia corpus it falls to rank 1,761 with 1,149. The pronoun tracks how conversational the writing is, not what the grammar demands.

faqs.question: Can I just answer 'yo también'?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the most common short reply. It is an ellipsis of the full clause, so it inherits whichever verb they used — with one exception: it cannot stand in for me haces falta, where the subject is the other person, not you.

faqs.question: Is 'a mí también' a correct reply to 'te extraño'?
faqs.answer: No. A mí is the prepositional form in the RAE's tonic-pronoun table, and te extraño has no prepositional slot for it — the verb is transitive and you would be the subject. A mí también belongs with verbs like gustar or hacer falta.

faqs.question: What does 'y yo a ti' mean?
faqs.answer: Literally 'and I, to you'. It is a compact reply to te extraño that fills the prepositional slot with a ti instead of restating the verb. It reads as warm and slightly literary, and it avoids the ambiguity of te extraño también entirely.

faqs.question: Does 'extrañar' or 'echar de menos' matter for the reply?
faqs.answer: Not for the pronoun. Both are transitive with the misser as subject, so both take yo también in the same position. The choice between them is regional rather than grammatical, and mirroring whichever one they used is the safer move.

faqs.question: Is 'yo también te extraño mucho' too strong?
faqs.answer: No — mucho is an ordinary intensifier here and adds no commitment beyond emphasis. If you want a shorter escalation, te extraño más ('I miss you more') is the standard playful reply and is extremely common in chat.

faqs.question: How is this different from saying 'I miss you too' in Italian or German?
faqs.answer: Every language in this lane solves it differently. Italian uses adjacency, so anche attaches to whatever it stands beside. German treats auch as a focus particle that reaches backwards. Dutch changes the pronoun itself. Spanish is the only one of the eight measured so far where the mechanism is a pronoun you are allowed to leave out.

faqs.question: Should I send a page instead of a message?
faqs.answer: Only if you have more than a line to say. Across the 214 miss-you pages measured on 2026-09-25, the median written letter was 88 words and the longest 1,024 — so a page suits a paragraph, not a four-word reply. Note also that the template's labels and prompts are in English.

article.contentMarkdown:
# I Miss You Too in Spanish: Which Reply Is Correct Depends on the Verb They Used

"I miss you too" has four common Spanish replies, and the one you may use is fixed by the verb the other person typed, not by preference. If they wrote *te extraño* or *te echo de menos*, answer **yo también te extraño** / **yo también te echo de menos**. If they wrote *me haces falta*, **yo también is ungrammatical** — you need *tú también me haces falta*. We have measured this lane from the product side too: 214 "I miss you" pages have been created on our /missyou-gf template since 2026-07-28, 4.1% of all 5,221 pages across 44 collections, and 43.5% of those senders password-protect the page before sharing it (93 of 214) — the most private segment we have measured anywhere on the platform.

The mechanism is not the one most guides describe: it is not about where *también* goes, but whether you write *yo* at all.

## The short answer, and the one rule the ranking pages skip

Spanish gives you a choice English does not have: the subject pronoun is optional. Because it is optional, writing it is a signal. That is the whole trick, and it is why *yo también te extraño* lands as "I, for my part, miss you too" rather than a flat echo.

The Real Academia Española's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* sets out the two slots plainly in its entry on [tonic personal pronouns](https://www.rae.es/dpd/pronombres%20personales%20t%C3%B3nicos): these are the pronouns that "pueden funcionar como sujeto (*Tú sabrás*) o como término de preposición". Its table gives first person singular as **yo** for the subject slot and **mí** for the prepositional slot.

So *yo también* adds you in the subject slot, and *a mí también* adds you in the prepositional slot. They are not stylistic variants. They answer different verbs.

## Why "yo" is the mechanism, and English has no equivalent

English requires a subject pronoun in a finite clause. You cannot write "miss you too" and have it mean the same thing as "I miss you too" in formal writing — the *I* is structural, so its presence carries no information.

Spanish does not require it. The verb ending on *extraño* already says first person singular, and the DPD table above lists *yo* only in the subject row — it has no other slot to occupy. Writing it is therefore elective, and elective material is read as contrastive. English speakers reach for "I too miss you" to get the same effect, which is why it sounds stiff.

That is the real asymmetry, and it is an asymmetry of **optionality**, not of placement.

## What the corpora actually show about *también*

I tested the placement claim rather than assuming it, and half of it failed. Spanish postposes *también* perfectly happily. In a census of 120 attested Spanish sentences [containing *también*](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/search?from=spa&to=eng&query=tambi%C3%A9n) drawn from Tatoeba (sampled 2026-09-28), the particle sits **sentence-initially in 36.7%, medially in 33.3%, and clause-finally in 30.0%** of cases. *¡Te extraño también!* and *¡Te echo de menos también!* are both attested sentences.

So the idea that Spanish "cannot put the additive particle at the end the way English does" is not true. It can, and does, roughly a third of the time.

The [Leipzig Corpora Collection](https://corpora.wortschatz-leipzig.de/en?corpusId=spa_news_2011_3M) gives the frequency side. In its 3-million-sentence Spanish news corpus, *también* is the 48th most frequent word with 87,096 occurrences, while *yo* is only 229th with 22,562. Switch to the Spanish Wikipedia corpus and *también* barely moves (rank 42), but *yo* collapses to rank 1,761 with 1,149 hits.

That gap is the finding. The particle is register-neutral; the pronoun is not.

## Register is why *yo también* dominates in chat

A 2025 study in the *Journal of Historical Sociolinguistics*, ["Orality and overtness: effects on Spanish subject use"](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12619655), built a diachronic Latin-American corpus (CorDELES) and found that how speech-like a text is significantly predicts overt subject pronoun use. Its four sample texts range from **2.9% to 22% overt subject pronouns**, and no corpus proportion exceeds 30%.

A text message is about as oral as written Spanish gets. That is why *yo también* feels normal in a reply and vanishingly rare in an encyclopedia entry.

There is a second reason your reply will mirror theirs. A 2025 paper in *Open Mind*, ["Hearing Pronouns Primes Speakers to Use Pronouns"](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11729791), found reference form is primed by recent exposure: **4 of 33 participants (12%) in the pronoun-prime condition produced no pronouns at all, against 22 of 35 (63%) in the name-prime condition**. Echoing the form your partner just used is the documented default, and here it is also the correct strategy.

## If they wrote *me haces falta*, *yo también* is wrong

This is the trap, and it is grammatical rather than regional. The DPD entry for [*faltar*](https://www.rae.es/dpd/faltar) states that in all its senses — including *hacer falta* — the verb **"es intransitivo"**. With *me haces falta*, the subject is *tú*: you are the one who is lacking, to me.

So there is no subject slot for *yo* to occupy. The reply is *tú también me haces falta*, or the neat elliptical *y tú a mí*. Put *yo también* in front of *me haces falta* and you have said something that does not parse.

The dative-slot reply *a mí también* belongs to that second verb family, not to *te extraño* — our Spanish-language page on [yo también te extraño](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/yo-tambien-te-extrano) works through that side in Spanish, with the RAE's *tampoco* ruling and a corpus count, and it is not a translation of this page.

## The four replies compared

| Reply | RAE slot it fills | Answers which verb | Attested in my Tatoeba census |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Yo también te extraño* | subject (*yo*) | *te extraño* / *te echo de menos* | yes |
| *Te extraño también* | none — particle only | same, but ambiguous in writing | yes |
| *Yo también* (alone) | subject (*yo*) | either, as an ellipsis | yes, 235 hits for the bare phrase |
| *Tú también me haces falta* | subject (*tú*) | *me haces falta* | *a mí también* frame attested, 47 hits |
| *Y yo a ti* | prepositional (*a ti*) | *te extraño* | yes, as an ellipsis |

*Te extraño también* is correct but under-specified: with nothing in the subject slot, it can be read as "I miss you as well as missing other people". That ambiguity is exactly the one English "I miss you too" has, which is the point — Spanish only escapes it when you spend the pronoun.

## A contradiction you can check in a page that ranks for this query

I measured the US English results for this keyword on 2026-09-28 using the harness WebSearch tool, not Google — our scripted DuckDuckGo route echoed the query back correctly and returned no parsed results, which is an IP-level block on our side rather than a property of the SERP. Nine results were visible. Five were forums, a social post or a dictionary scraper (Quora, HiNative, a Facebook post, Tureng, and the Wikipedia article for a 2019 film with the same name); four were content pages.

One of those four, QuillBot's Spanish blog, states the recipe for this exact phrase as adding "the subject pronoun *yo*" plus the adverb *también*. Its own table then gives three rows — *Yo también te echo de menos*, *Yo también te extraño*, and **"También me haces falta"**, with no *yo*, and no explanation of why the third row breaks the rule the page just stated.

The reason is the DPD's intransitive ruling above. The page is not wrong in its output; it is wrong in the rule it hands the reader, who will write something ungrammatical if they apply it consistently. None of the nine results explains the split.

## Eight languages, eight different mechanisms

This reply lane has now been measured across eight languages, and no two solve "too" the same way. Italian uses adjacency — *anche* attaches to whatever it stands next to. German treats *auch* as a focus particle that reaches backwards. Dutch changes the **pronoun**, making the full form *jou* obligatory. Polish attaches *też* to whatever carries the sentence accent. Portuguese has free position with phrasal accent doing the work. Russian splits *тоже* from *также*. Indonesian permits *juga* on either side of the verb. Spanish is the only one where the mechanism is a pronoun you may legally omit.

English is the odd one out differently: one strategy, a clause-final *too*, and no way to disambiguate it in writing at all.

## What our own numbers show, and what they cannot

Across those 214 miss-you pages, the median letter is **88 words** and the longest is 1,024 — so the reply people actually send at length is a paragraph, not a phrase. Recipients tapped the "hug" control 1,434 times across 138 of the 214 pages, meaning 64.5% of pages received at least one.

Three caveats are not optional. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are **pickers with defaults**, so their fill rates are not sender choices and nothing here is derived from them. *viewCount* counts page views, not unique visitors — one person reopening a page twenty times is twenty views. And n = 214 over roughly two months supports no seasonal claim whatsoever.

One more that matters on a page about Spanish: the database records **which template was opened, never who received it**, and nothing in it is segmented by language or country. None of these figures is a Spanish figure. Do not read them as one.

## The page is in English, and when to skip it

If you want to send more than a line, the [miss-you page for a partner](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) is the template those 214 pages were built on — a letter, memories, open-when notes and a countdown on one link. Its labels, prompts and furniture are **in English**. Your Spanish will sit inside an English frame, and if your recipient reads no English at all, that frame will be visible to them.

For a long-distance reply that repeats rather than arrives once, [Streak](https://subhsandesh.in/streak) suits better: one tap a day each, and after a hundred days you have a diary neither of you meant to write. That is a closer fit than a single page when the missing is ongoing rather than acute.

And the honest limit: if the right answer is four words in a chat window, none of this helps. Write *yo también te extraño*, or *tú también me haces falta* if that is the verb they used, and close the tab — you can [browse the other templates](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) another day.

structuralLimitations: MY PROMPT'S FRAMING WAS HALF WRONG AND IS CORRECTED IN THE BODY. The prompt asserted that Spanish 'cannot postpose the additive particle onto the object the way English too does'. Measured: in 120 attested Tatoeba sentences containing también, 30.0% are clause-final, and both '¡Te extraño también!' and '¡Te echo de menos también!' are attested. Spanish postposes it freely. The prompt's CONCLUSION survives but on a different mechanism: it is not también that forces a subject reading, it is yo, which the RAE's tonic-pronoun table licenses only in the subject slot and which Spanish may omit entirely. The asymmetry with English is optionality, not placement.

The 120-sentence census is a sample, not the whole set. Tatoeba's API reports the count for 'también' as exactly 1000, which is a cap rather than a true total, so no population proportion may be derived; the percentages describe the sample only. The sample is also relevance-ordered, which biases it toward short sentences.

Tatoeba phrase search is fuzzy: the query "también te extraño" returned 'También te extrañamos', a different inflection. Per-phrase counts in this post are therefore reported as attestation (present / absent) rather than as frequencies, except where the whole-corpus census is cited.

The Leipzig Spanish corpora are from 2011 and are news and encyclopedic prose. They cannot speak directly to text-message Spanish; the orality paper is what licenses the extrapolation, and it is an inference, not a measurement of chat.

No first-party figure in this post is Spanish, Mexican or Latin American. The gifts database records which template was opened and never who received it, and it is not segmented by language or country. This is disclosed in body prose.

n = 214 miss-you pages over roughly two months from 2026-07-28 supports no seasonal claim; viewCount is page views, not unique visitors; and the city, background-music and 'together since' fields are pickers with defaults, so none of them is used here as evidence of a sender's choice.

The RAE's CORPES XXI and CREA return 403 to scripts and Corpus del Español requires a login, so no Academy corpus frequency could be obtained. The DPD's own entries and the Leipzig corpora were substituted; a CORPES count would be the stronger instrument and remains open.

QuillBot is named but deliberately not linked, per the no-competitor-links rule. A reader who wants to check the contradiction must search the page themselves; the contradiction is stated precisely enough to be found.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on the nine results I measured that makes the reply depend on the verb rather than on the particle, and it is the only one anywhere in this lane that reports the negative result against its own commissioning framing: Spanish postposes también in 30.0% of a 120-sentence census, so the 'Spanish cannot postpose' story is wrong and the asymmetry is the optional subject pronoun instead. The DPD faltar ruling gives it a hard, checkable claim — yo también after me haces falta is ungrammatical — that no ranking result states and one ranking result's stated rule actively contradicts. Against that: the incumbents are SpanishDict and established Spanish-teaching sites with years of authority on a high-volume English query, the first-party data is not Spanish and cannot be made so, and the corpus sample is 120 sentences from a relevance-ordered API with a capped total. Expect this to be cited by an answer engine for the verb-licensing rule long before it ranks, if it ranks at all.
